planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to wet soil in full sun; Wyndley is an RHS Award of Garden Merit holder prized for its unusually compact, early-blooming habit and strong mildew resistance.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun; Wyndley bears coppery-yellow, reflexed rays flecked with orange and red around a dark brown disk, flowering noticeably earlier (from June) than most sneezeweed cultivars and continuing into August. Its short, sturdy stature is among the most compact of any Helenium autumnale selection, making it useful at the front of a border or in containers without staking. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent flower heads to encourage continued bloom. The plant shows notably good resistance to powdery mildew compared with taller Helenium cultivars, and its nectar- and pollen-rich flowers draw bumblebees and other late-season pollinators.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rubinzwerg (German-bred, RHS AGM) is intolerant of drought and performs best where soil moisture is reliable through summer.

directions: Plant in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Rubinzwerg produces deep ruby-red to crimson flowers that fade attractively to coppery orange as they age, set off by umber-brown central cones and blue-green foliage. Bred by the German nursery Zur Linden, it is shorter and sturdier-stemmed than older tall sneezeweed selections, rarely requiring staking, and blooms over a long window from late summer into early fall. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season, as the cultivar does not tolerate drought well and may defoliate from the base if stressed late in the season. Divide every three to four years in spring; the long bloom period makes it valuable for late-season bumblebees and specialist Helenium-foraging bees.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Kupferzwerg is a compact German-bred cultivar distinct from the larger, patented 'Mardi Gras' selection.

directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Kupferzwerg bears strongly reflexed, coppery reddish-brown petals arranged around a dark brown domed disk, flowering from midsummer through early fall. Its compact, bushy habit and sturdy stems make it well suited to mid-border placement without staking. Water during dry spells, as consistent moisture produces the strongest flower display and reduces stress-related foliage decline. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor; the long bloom season provides a valuable late nectar source for bumblebees and other native pollinators.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to wet, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Flammenrad is an older German-bred cultivar valued for reliable disease resistance and a long midsummer-to-fall bloom season.

directions: Plant in fertile, average to wet, well-drained soil in full sun; Flammenrad opens with fiery orange-red petals that fade toward orange and yellow as flowers age, surrounding a chocolate-brown, gold-dusted central disk. It is a taller, classic-form sneezeweed, so stake or grow among sturdier neighbors in exposed or windy sites. The long midsummer-to-fall bloom period, combined with good resistance to insect pests and disease, makes it a reliable choice for cutting gardens and pollinator borders alike. Divide every three to four years in spring to rejuvenate clumps; deer generally avoid it, while bees and butterflies visit heavily.

planting.note: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water before direct sowing in average to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; smooth tick trefoil tolerates poor, sandy soils typical of open woodland edges and dry fields.

directions: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water before direct sowing into average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth tick trefoil is a slender, upright native legume bearing small white-to-pink or pale purple pea-like flowers in loose branching clusters from July through September. As with other Desmodium species, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, helping enrich dry, sandy, or nutrient-poor soils found along woodland edges and old fields where it grows wild from New England south to Florida and west to Missouri and Texas. Its seed pods break into hooked, single-seeded segments that cling to clothing and fur for dispersal. The foliage serves as larval host for several skipper and sulphur butterfly species, and the flowers draw a range of small native bees during late summer.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water before direct sowing in dry to average, sandy or well-drained soil in full sun in spring; stiff tick trefoil (formerly classified as Desmodium rigidum) thrives in open, dry woods and sandy fields.

directions: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water before direct sowing into dry to average, sandy or well-drained soil in full sun; stiff tick trefoil is a wiry, upright native legume, formerly named Desmodium rigidum, that bears small pink-to-pale-yellow pea-like flowers over an unusually long season from spring into fall. Native from Colorado and Texas east to Connecticut and south to Alabama, it thrives in dry, open woods, sandy fields, and other low-fertility sites where it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and improves soil over time. Its hooked seed segments cling to fur and clothing for dispersal, the classic tick-trefoil trait. Leave plants unmowed through summer where used in meadow or prairie restorations, as the foliage is a larval host for several skipper butterfly species and the flowers attract small native bees.
